results.title: Jayson Shin
results.content: - I spent this past weekend doing something every founder should do more often: getting out from behind the computer. Instead of writing code, I drove to Hoboken and spent the afternoon talking to people. I visited 18 local bars to discuss potential partnerships for Destiny Rings, then walked along the waterfront interviewing strangers about modern dating and technology. One thing became very clear: People are longing for connection. Real, authentic connection. Despite all the advances in technology, I kept hearing the same frustrations: • Endless swiping • Algorithms deciding who you see • Falsified profiles • Misaligned intentions • Safety concerns As founders, it's easy to convince ourselves we know exactly what customers want. The harder—and far more valuable—thing to do is listen. [...] - Lately I’ve been thinking a lot about how technology changed the way people interact in real life. People are surrounded by other people constantly — cities, bars, gyms, coffee shops, events — yet spontaneous interaction feels rarer than ever. My theory is that dating apps solved “discovery,” but unintentionally trained people to wait for digital validation before initiating real-world interaction. A lot of people now subconsciously think: “If they were interested, we probably would’ve matched already.” That shift in behavior is actually what led me to start building Destiny Rings — a proximity-based social platform built around Bluetooth-enabled smart rings. The idea is simple: When compatible people are physically nearby, the ring gives a subtle signal through a paired app experience.
